## Exercise 4.1: Fix the rule {#ex-4.1}

The first problem stops the job before anything runs:

<!-- GENERATE: stopB-count-reads-broken | stopping-points/stopB | cat >> Snakefile <<'EOF'
rule count_reads:
    input:
        bam = OUT + "/{sample}/{sample}_filtered.bam",
    output:
        OUT + "/{sample}/{sample}_read_count.txt",
    log:
        LOGS + "/count_reads/{sample}.log",
    threads: 2
    shell:
        """
        samtools view -c -@ {threads} {input.bam} | awk '{print "{wildcards.sample}", $1}' > {output} 2> {log}
        """
EOF
snakemake -n -p output/HCT116_CTCF_1/HCT116_CTCF_1_read_count.txt 2>&1 | sed -n '/^RuleException/,$p' || true -->

{{< generated name="stopB-count-reads-broken" command="false" >}}

The awk program's braces are read as a Snakemake placeholder, and
`{print "{wildcards.sample}"` is not a valid one. The message is less clear
than the `NameError` in the lesson, because here a real placeholder sits
inside the awk braces. The fix is the same: double awk's braces, and leave
Snakemake's single.

The second problem does not raise an error, which makes it worse. `2> {log}`
at the end of the line belongs to `awk` only. If samtools fails or warns, its
message goes to the terminal (or the cluster's job log), not to the rule's
log. Redirect each command:

```{.python filename="Snakefile"}
    shell:
        """
        samtools view -c -@ {threads} {input.bam} 2> {log} \
            | awk '{{print "{wildcards.sample}", $1}}' > {output} 2>> {log}
        """
```

- `2> {log}` right after the samtools command catches its stderr and starts
  the log fresh.
- `{{print ...}}` becomes `{print ...}` for awk, while `{wildcards.sample}`
  in between is still filled in by Snakemake.
- `2>> {log}` appends awk's stderr instead of overwriting samtools'.

<!-- GENERATE: stopB-count-reads-fixed | stopping-points/stopB | cat >> Snakefile <<'EOF'
rule count_reads:
    input:
        bam = OUT + "/{sample}/{sample}_filtered.bam",
    output:
        OUT + "/{sample}/{sample}_read_count.txt",
    log:
        LOGS + "/count_reads/{sample}.log",
    threads: 2
    shell:
        """
        samtools view -c -@ {threads} {input.bam} 2> {log} \
            | awk '{{print "{wildcards.sample}", $1}}' > {output} 2>> {log}
        """
EOF
snakemake --cores 4 output/HCT116_CTCF_1/HCT116_CTCF_1_read_count.txt > /dev/null 2>&1; cat output/HCT116_CTCF_1/HCT116_CTCF_1_read_count.txt -->

```bash
snakemake --cores 4 output/HCT116_CTCF_1/HCT116_CTCF_1_read_count.txt
cat output/HCT116_CTCF_1/HCT116_CTCF_1_read_count.txt
```

{{< generated name="stopB-count-reads-fixed" command="false" >}}

24,434 reads survive filtering for CTCF replicate 1, out of 28,634 that went
in. Strict mode (`set -euo pipefail`) is what makes a samtools failure fail
the job here; the log is what tells you why.

## Exercise 4.2: Add a log and a benchmark {#ex-4.2}

```{.python filename="Snakefile"}
rule filter:
    input:
        bam = OUT + "/{sample}/{sample}_aligned.bam",
        blacklist = DATA + "/reference/blacklist.bed.gz",
    output:
        bam = OUT + "/{sample}/{sample}_filtered.bam",
        bai = OUT + "/{sample}/{sample}_filtered.bam.bai",
        flagstat = OUT + "/{sample}/{sample}_aligned_flagstat.tsv",
        markdup = OUT + "/{sample}/{sample}_markdup.txt",
    log:
        OUT + "/logs/filter/{sample}.log",                                    # <1>
    benchmark:
        OUT + "/benchmarks/filter/{sample}.tsv",                              # <2>
    shell:
        """
        samtools flagstat -O tsv {input.bam} > {output.flagstat} 2> {log}     # <3>
        samtools view -u -q {MIN_MAPQ} -F {EXCLUDE_FLAGS} {input.bam} 2>> {log} \
            | bedtools intersect -v -abam stdin -b {input.blacklist} 2>> {log} \
            | samtools markdup -r -f {output.markdup} - {output.bam} 2>> {log}  # <4>
        samtools index {output.bam} 2>> {log}
        """
```

1. Same `{sample}` wildcard as the outputs. Every wildcard in `log:` and
   `benchmark:` must also appear in the output, or Snakemake cannot fill it.
2. One TSV per job, written by Snakemake itself. Nothing in the command
   refers to it.
3. The first command creates the log with `2>`. Its stdout already goes to
   the flagstat file, so only stderr is redirected.
4. Every other command appends with `2>>`, each in its own place in the pipe.
   `samtools markdup` warns about library size estimates on single-end data;
   that warning now lands in the log instead of the terminal.

Stopping point B's version also has `threads:` and moves the two settings into
`params:`:

{{< snippet repo="stopB" file="Snakefile" rule="filter" >}}

## Exercise 4.3: Read a benchmark {#ex-4.3}

Compare `cpu_time` with `s`. In the benchmark shown on the lesson page,
bowtie2-build ran for a few seconds of wall-clock time and used roughly twice
as many CPU seconds, so on average it kept about two cores busy, not four.
`mean_load` says the same in percent (about 200, where 400 would be four full
cores). The exact numbers change from run to run.

That is normal for bowtie2-build on a small genome: parts of the build are
single-threaded. `threads: 4` is still right, because the threaded parts get
faster. What you learn from the benchmark is not to raise it further.

To compare rules after a full run, read every benchmark into one table. In R:

```{.r filename="bench.R"}
files <- list.files("output/benchmarks", pattern = "\\.tsv$",
                    recursive = TRUE, full.names = TRUE)                  # <1>
bench <- files |>
  lapply(\(f) cbind(rule = basename(dirname(f)), read.delim(f))) |>     # <2>
  do.call(what = rbind)
bench |>
  aggregate(cbind(s, max_rss) ~ rule, data = _, FUN = max) |>          # <3>
  print(row.names = FALSE)
```

1. `output/benchmarks/<rule>/<sample>.tsv`, one file per job.
2. The folder name is the rule name, so it becomes a column.
3. The slowest job and the largest memory peak per rule.

One run of stopping point B on a 4-core Linux machine gave:

```text
            rule      s max_rss
           align 2.5829  109.15
          bigwig 0.4643    9.36
   bowtie2_index 4.6919   52.27
      call_peaks 0.4309   10.57
 consensus_peaks 0.0201    3.45
          fastqc 4.3722  242.85
          filter 1.6987   21.05
```

FastQC used the most memory (about 240 MB per job). It is a Java program and
starts a whole JVM for every FASTQ. On the full genome the alignment numbers
would be far larger; on the 5 Mb course window they are tiny.

Treat numbers for jobs that last a second or less with suspicion. Snakemake
samples the job's processes while they run, and a job that is over before the
first samples are taken can show `cpu_time` of 0 and a `max_rss` that is only
the shell. In this run, every `bigwig` and `call_peaks` job reported
`cpu_time` 0.00, which is not what deepTools and MACS3 really used.

## Exercise 4.4: What does `--rerun-triggers mtime` change? {#ex-4.4}

`qvalue` is a `param` of `call_peaks`. With the default triggers:

<!-- GENERATE: stopB-qvalue-rerun | stopping-points/stopB | snakemake --cores 4 > /dev/null 2>&1; sed -i 's/qvalue: 0.01/qvalue: 0.05/' config/RegConfig.yaml && snakemake -n 2>&1 | awk '/^Job stats/ && !done {on=1} on {print} /^total/ && on {on=0; done=1}'; echo; echo '$ snakemake -n --rerun-triggers mtime'; snakemake -n --rerun-triggers mtime 2>&1 | tail -1 -->

{{< generated name="stopB-qvalue-rerun" command="false" >}}

- All 6 `call_peaks` jobs, with the reason `Params have changed since last
  execution`.
- All 3 `consensus_peaks` jobs, because their inputs will be new.
- `all`.
- Nothing upstream: no alignment, filtering or FastQC, and no bigWigs (they
  do not use peaks).

With `--rerun-triggers mtime`, nothing. No file is newer than anything that
depends on it, and timestamps are all that is checked.

The second run leaves you with `config/RegConfig.yaml` saying 0.05 and every
file under `output/peaks/` and `output/consensus/` made with 0.01. Nothing on
disk tells you so. That is the risk: `mtime` is right when you know the change
cannot affect results (a comment, a log path, a switch to conda for the same
tool versions), and wrong for any change to a setting.
